analysis.one_liner: Hands a mining company 6,650 acres of national forest in Minnesota in exchange for other company-owned land.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 309-99, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would order the U.S. Department of Agriculture to trade about 6,650 acres of Superior National Forest land to Poly Met Mining in exchange for about 6,690 acres of company-owned forest land in Minnesota. The federal land is the proposed site of Poly Met's NorthMet copper-nickel mine, and once traded it becomes private land open to mining under state and local rules. The bill locks in the 2015 government appraisals with no reappraisal and makes the exchange mandatory within 90 days of enactment, taking the decision out of the hands of land managers.
analysis.who_benefits: Poly Met Mining, which would receive 6,650 acres of national forest land containing its proposed NorthMet mine site, at fixed 2015 appraised values with no reappraisal allowed, and with no equalization payment owed. The public also gains: the company's 6,690 acres become national forest with public access, and Poly Met must reimburse the government's exchange costs.

how_it_helps.text: For Poly Met, it converts 6,650 acres of national forest land at the site of its proposed NorthMet copper-nickel mine into private land, usable for mining, and makes the exchange legally mandatory rather than discretionary.
It exempts the deal's 2015 appraisals from reappraisal and waives the government's right to revalue, shielding the company's side of the bargain from later challenge.
For the public, the company's 6,690 acres would enter the national forest and gain public access, and the company must reimburse the government's survey and appraisal costs.

analysis.who_pays: The public, which gives up permanent title to 6,650 acres of federal forest land, including the site of a proposed copper-nickel mine, with the trade valued at fixed 2015 appraisals and no reappraisal permitted.
analysis.who_pays_short: Users of the Superior National Forest

drawbacks.text: The bill locks in November 2015 appraisals and bars any reappraisal, so if the land the public gives away (the site of the proposed NorthMet copper-nickel mine) turns out to be worth far more than appraised, there is no chance to correct the balance.

Once conveyed, the federal land becomes private and available for any lawful use under mining laws, and the bill overrides any conflicting terms in the Forest Service's own Record of Decision, so the Forest Service loses discretion over the deal it approved.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public did gain public forest access and consolidated federal land, and Poly Met covered the transaction costs. But the binding constraint Congress removed was the reappraisal that would have tested whether the public was getting fair value, and the bill made the executive exchange legally unavoidable rather than voluntary. For a one-company transfer of federal land to enable a copper-nickel mine in a sensitive watershed, the design tilted toward the company.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by a wide margin, but the Senate referred it to the Agriculture Committee and never voted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Natural Resources reported the bill 26-10 in July 2017, and the full House passed it 309-99 on November 28, 2017 under a rule suspending normal procedures.
The Senate received the bill on November 29, 2017 and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry, where it sat with no further action.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 without the Senate voting, so the bill died there; the Forest Service's administrative exchange continued separately outside Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Poly Met and other companies pressing for the NorthMet mine gained time but got nothing new; the public kept the federal forest land, and opponents of the mine gained because the bill's shortcuts never took effect. The Senate's inaction preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept the forest land; the bill died

industries.note: The bill hands one specific company title to 6,650 acres of federal forest land containing its proposed mine site, at fixed 2015 appraised values with no reappraisal. Poly Met as a public-beneficiary company is best understood as part of the metals-mining industry it would join.

industries.industry: Copper-nickel / sulfide mining regulation and the outdoors-recreation economy of northern Minnesota
industries.note: The exchange removes federal control from the mine-site land, easing development of a sulfide mine whose waste risks water quality; fishing, tourism, and recreation economies around the Boundary Waters region bear the downstream risk. The public does gain some new forest acreage and access, which cuts the other way.
The public gains 6,690 acres added to the national forest, reduced boundary mileage to manage, and cost reimbursement from Poly Met, though it surrenders 6,650 acres including the mine site.
